title: How to Replace a Light Switch: Step-by-Step Guide
question: How do I replace a light switch?
summary: To replace a light switch, shut off the breaker, test that the wires are dead, and move each wire to the matching screw on the new switch. A standard switch takes 15 to 30 minutes and costs about $2 to $20. Buy the same kind you are taking out: single-pole if one switch controls the light, 3-way if two switches control it. Dimmers and smart switches have their own wiring rules, so follow the sheet that comes in the box.

commonCauses.cause: The switch is worn out. The toggle feels loose or mushy, sticks, or the light flickers or only works some of the time.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Put in a new bulb first. If the new bulb still flickers or cuts out when you move the toggle, the switch or one of its connections is failing.

commonCauses.cause: You want an upgrade: a rocker (Decora-style) switch, a dimmer, a timer, a motion sensor, or a smart switch.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Check two things before you buy. A dimmer needs bulbs marked dimmable. Many smart switches need a neutral wire, which is usually a bundle of white wires joined with a wire nut at the back of the box.

commonCauses.cause: A loose wire. Wires pushed into the small holes on the back of a switch (push-in or "back-stab" terminals) can loosen over time, and so can a screw that was never tightened fully.
commonCauses.quickCheck: With the breaker off and the wires tested dead, pull the switch out and look. Wires in the back holes instead of under the side screws are worth moving to the screws when you replace the switch.

commonCauses.cause: The switch buzzes, crackles, feels warm, or sparks when you flip it. This points to a loose connection or failing contacts inside the switch.
commonCauses.quickCheck: A standard switch should never feel warm. A dimmer can feel slightly warm in normal use. If you hear crackling or see sparks, turn the breaker off now. If you then find scorch marks or melted insulation, call an electrician.

fixes: Buy the right switch. Look at the old one. A single-pole switch has two brass screws plus a green ground screw, and the toggle says ON and OFF. A 3-way switch has three screws plus ground (one screw is darker, the "common"), and the toggle has no ON or OFF. A 4-way switch has four screws. Match the amp rating stamped on the old switch, which is usually 15 amps.
Turn off the power. Turn the light on, then switch breakers off one at a time until it goes dark. Leave that breaker off and put tape over it so no one turns it back on while you work.

Test that the power is off. Hold your voltage tester to an outlet you know is live to prove it works. Take off the cover plate and hold the tester to every wire and every screw in the box, not only the ones on the switch. Then test the live outlet again to make sure the tester did not fail. Only touch the wires when every test in the box stays silent.
Take out the old switch. Remove the two mounting screws and gently pull the switch out of the box. Take a clear photo of which wire goes to which screw before you disconnect anything.

Check for a white wire on the switch. In many homes one cable runs from the light to the switch, and its white wire is used as a hot wire. It should be marked with black or red tape. Treat it as hot, keep it on the switch, and add a band of black tape if it is not marked. Leave any bundle of white wires joined by a wire nut alone unless your new switch needs a neutral.

Move the wires one at a time. For a single-pole switch, put the two hot wires on the two brass screws. Either wire can go on either screw. Put the bare copper or green wire on the green ground screw. Strip about 3/4 inch of insulation, bend a hook, wrap it clockwise about three-quarters of the way around the screw, and tighten it firmly. Leviton lists 14 to 18 inch-pounds for its side screws.
Use the side screws, not the push-in holes, when you can. Leviton push-in holes accept only 14-gauge solid copper wire. A 20-amp circuit uses thicker 12-gauge wire, which must go under the screws.

For a 3-way switch, find the wire on the darker "common" screw of the old switch and put it on the common screw of the new one. The other two wires are travelers. They go on the two brass screws in either order.

For a dimmer or smart switch, follow the maker's wiring sheet. Many smart switches mark one wire "line" (from the breaker) and one "load" (to the light), and many need the neutral. On a 3-way circuit a smart switch usually needs a matching companion switch or remote from the same brand. Standard dimmers are for permanently installed lights only. Do not use one to control an outlet or a ceiling fan motor.

If there is no ground wire, look at the box. A metal box that is grounded through metal conduit or armored cable grounds the switch through its mounting screws. If there is no ground path at all, the electrical code allows a replacement switch only with a plastic, non-burning cover plate and plastic screws, or on a circuit with GFCI protection. If you are unsure, ask an electrician.

Fold the wires back into the box, screw the switch to the box, and put the cover plate on. Turn the breaker back on and test the light. If it does not work, turn the breaker off, test again, and compare the wiring to your photo.
diyVsPro: A careful homeowner can replace a standard single-pole or 3-way switch. The rule that keeps it safe is simple: breaker off, then test every wire. Call a licensed electrician if the wire is aluminum (dull silver, common in homes wired from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s; the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission says not to repair it yourself), if you see scorching or melted insulation, if the wires are too short or the box is too crowded to fit the new switch, if the box holds more cables than any diagram you can find, or if you cannot get your tester to show the wires are dead. Rules on who may do electrical work differ by state and town, so check with your local building department. An electrician typically charges $50 to $150 to replace a standard switch, $70 to $200 for a 3-way, and $80 to $250 or more for a dimmer or smart switch, and many add a $75 to $125 service call fee.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: $2-$20 for a standard switch, $6-$40 for a dimmer, $20-$100 for a smart switch, plus about $15-$30 for a voltage tester if you do not have one. Electrician: $50-$150 for a standard switch, $70-$200 for a 3-way, $80-$250 or more for a dimmer or smart switch; many charge a $75-$125 service call fee.
timeEstimate: 15-30 minutes to swap a single-pole switch for the same kind. 30-60 minutes for a 3-way, dimmer, or smart switch, or if it is your first time.
safetyNote: Turn off the breaker, not just the wall switch. Then test before you touch anything. Check your tester on an outlet you know is live, test every wire and screw in the box, then check the tester on the live outlet again. A switch box can hold wires from a second circuit that is still on, so one quiet wire does not prove the box is dead. Stop and call a licensed electrician if you find dull silver (aluminum) wire, scorched or melted insulation, a switch that was hot to the touch, or wiring that does not match your photo or this guide. Work on the panel or on any 240-volt circuit is always a job for an electrician.
toolsParts: Replacement switch of the same kind and amp rating (single-pole, 3-way, dimmer, or smart)
Voltage tester (a non-contact pen tester, or a two-lead tester for a surer reading)
Needle-nose pliers to bend wire hooks
Wire strippers, if a wire end is nicked or too short
Electrical tape to mark wires and re-mark a white wire used as a hot
Masking tape to cover the breaker you turned off
Phone to photograph the wiring before you disconnect it
New cover plate (plastic if the box has no ground)
